title: Analysis of Cork-Based Networking

jokes.text: Is deforestation on the list? I, for one, am glad that this is happening.
jokes.setup: Jeff asks who wants to list Greendale emergencies, implying civic responsibility
jokes.punchline: Shirley expresses genuine satisfaction about deforestation, undercutting the premise entirely
jokes.explanation: Quick absurdist beat — the character expressing delight at something ostensibly bad subverts the earnest committee meeting setup. Functional but not especially developed.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff Winger
dialogue.line: Our committee is like a fantasy house.

dialogue.speaker: Britta Perry
dialogue.line: You mean like Game of Thrones?

dialogue.speaker: Jeff Winger
dialogue.line: No, more like... House of the Dragon... wait, I mean House Targaryen... actually, House of Cards.

jokes.text: What this school needs is a band of heroes. Champions willing to rise up and 'Get all those potatoes out of the gym.'
jokes.setup: Jeff grandiosely frames himself as rallying a heroic committee for a noble cause
jokes.punchline: The 'heroic' cause is literally just removing potatoes from the gym — bathetically mundane
jokes.explanation: Classic Jeff deflation joke — his grandiose rhetorical mode applied to an absurdly trivial task. The specificity of 'potatoes out of the gym' earns the laugh. Character-integrated and well-structured.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff Winger
dialogue.line: What makes this show great is the writing, the characters, the heart—

dialogue.speaker: Pierce Hawthorne
dialogue.line: And the incest.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff Winger
dialogue.line: No, Pierce, not the incest.

jokes.text: Like House Vogadash in the HBO series, Bloodlines of Conquest. — 'That is a good show. They really get the incest right.'
jokes.setup: Abed makes a reference to a fantasy show, the group enthusiastically agrees
jokes.punchline: The praise singles out 'the incest' as the show's distinguishing quality, delivered with complete sincerity
jokes.explanation: Sharp Game of Thrones parody joke. The deadpan delivery of 'they really get the incest right' as a sincere compliment is the entire joke, and it lands because of the economy — no explanation needed. The group endorsing it makes it communal.

jokes.text: It's got betrayal, boobs, espionage, dragons. Oh wait, dragons? Is that a spoiler? I just started season one.
jokes.setup: Shirley enthusiastically lists the show's appealing elements
jokes.punchline: Jeff interrupts worried about dragon spoilers — the most fantastical and 'obvious' element is treated as the sensitive spoiler while nothing else gives him pause
jokes.explanation: Good misdirection: Jeff is unbothered by betrayal, boobs, espionage, but dragons — the most iconic fantasy element — trip his spoiler anxiety. It sets up the running gag with Abed's spoiler plot thread.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: This is ridiculous. I can't even talk about what happened in Game of Thrones without someone yelling at me about spoilers.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: It's like we're living in some kind of fantasy world where people actually care about spoiler warnings.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Oh wait, we are. A literal fantasy world is the show everyone's upset about.

jokes.text: I don't start watching shows until they're so popular, watching is no longer a statement.
jokes.setup: Group discussion about being current on the show
jokes.punchline: Britta articulates her media consumption philosophy — she intentionally waits until watching has no cultural cachet, perfectly satirizing hipster/contrarian posturing
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best lines. It perfectly encapsulates Britta's contrarian anti-hipster-but-also-hipster personality in a single self-defeating sentence. 'Watching is no longer a statement' is precisely the kind of thing only Britta would say and believe is a reasonable position. High quotability, tight construction, exceptional character integration. Approaches the 8.0 anchor benchmark.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff Winger
dialogue.line: If you read those books, you're going to spoil the show for yourself.

dialogue.speaker: Abed Nadir
dialogue.line: That's insane.

jokes.text: You're behind, so we have to live in a world where there's no dragons? Do we have to pretend that Lord Stevarios is still alive?
jokes.setup: Jeff is worried about dragon spoilers from season one
jokes.punchline: Abed flips it — his being up-to-date means everyone ELSE must manage their ignorance, not him. He casually drops a character death as though it's already in the past.
jokes.explanation: Good Abed logic — he frames the social obligation as running in reverse, which is very true to his character and to real spoiler culture debates. The accidental (?) death spoiler drop is the bonus punch.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: I don't watch shows because they're popular. I watch shows because they're interesting to me, regardless of what everyone else thinks.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Actually, if anything, I'm more likely to watch something if nobody else is watching it. That's where the real value is.

jokes.text: An insane person would do that.
jokes.setup: Jeff threatens to read all the books and spoil everything for Abed as revenge
jokes.punchline: Abed simply categorizes this as insane behavior — matter-of-fact, no escalation, the flattest possible dismissal
jokes.explanation: Perfect economy — five words that completely defuse Jeff's threat by refusing to treat it as credible. Abed's clinical literalism is the joke. Very character-specific.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: I need someone to hang a bulletin board in the study room.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: I'll do it.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Great. Try not to make it a drive-by.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: What?

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: You know, just hang it and leave. Don't turn it into some kind of gang activity.

jokes.text: No. / Fine, I'll do it. / I will be on that committee. / Me too.
jokes.setup: Dean asks for volunteers for the decorating committee
jokes.punchline: Jeff's immediate 'No' triggers an instant pile-on of volunteers, implying everyone was waiting to volunteer only after Jeff refused — or wanted to avoid being left alone with Annie doing all the work
jokes.explanation: Quick ensemble beat. The comedic logic works — nobody wants to volunteer until they fear being stuck with Annie's workaholic energy — but it's lightly sketched.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Wait, so the king is actually the queen's brother, who was switched at birth with the stable boy, who is also the wizard's son?

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Dude, what?

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: And the stable boy's mother is the queen's secret twin sister.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: That doesn't even make sense!

jokes.text: Are you guys volunteering because I'll do all the work? — 'I wouldn't.' 'Not at all.' 'I don't care enough to lie, so no.'
jokes.setup: Annie suspects the volunteers are freeloading on her work ethic
jokes.punchline: Two characters offer transparently hollow denials; Duncan breaks the pattern by confessing he doesn't even care enough to lie
jokes.explanation: The escalation from obvious lying to confessed apathy is the structure here, and it works. Duncan's 'I don't care enough to lie' is the kicker — it's character-specific honesty played as a virtue of laziness.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Can I borrow some tools to hang a bulletin board?

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: No.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Okay.

jokes.text: A bulletin board fell down in the cafeteria a couple months ago. — 'I'll give it a drive-by.'
jokes.setup: The Dean presents the bulletin board task as something that can be assigned
jokes.punchline: Hickey agrees to 'give it a drive-by' — the most minimal, noncommittal commitment possible for a trivially simple task
jokes.explanation: Establishes Hickey's laziness/cynicism with an appropriately deflating phrase. 'Drive-by' for hanging a bulletin board is a good word choice. Functional character establishment.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: I need you to fill out this form.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: But don't talk while you're doing it.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: I'm deaf.

jokes.text: Oh, no. [long pause as the star wall is revealed] Yeah. Yeah, yeah, yeah.
jokes.setup: The Dean announces a 'task wall' where every completed task gets a star — delivered with great pride
jokes.punchline: The reaction shot (implied by the gap and 'Oh, no') reveals the wall is probably a sad, childlike, over-the-top display — the group's resigned 'Yeah. Yeah, yeah, yeah.' confirms the visual absurdity
jokes.explanation: The 30-second pause (00:01:59 to 00:02:29) followed by resigned affirmations is a pure visual/reaction beat. The Dean's pride versus everyone else's despair at the childish gold-star system is communicated entirely without dialogue. Good use of the mockumentary format's silent beats.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Okay, if you can really read lips, tell me what I'm saying right now.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: You're saying gibberish.

jokes.text: Brince Ironstone's daughter is his mother!
jokes.setup: We cut to Abed, apparently having watched ahead in the fantasy show, delivering a spoiler to no one in particular
jokes.punchline: The content of the spoiler — incest of the most convoluted variety — is both a parody of prestige fantasy and a callback to the incest compliment from earlier
jokes.explanation: Perfectly economical — eleven words containing both a convoluted Game of Thrones-style twist and an incest joke. The gleeful randomness of this cut-away moment, with Abed alone making the discovery, is very Community. High quotability.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Hi, I'm here for the census.

dialogue.speaker: Census Worker
dialogue.line: Great! Can you tell me your name?

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: I'm deaf, so you'll need to speak up.

dialogue.speaker: Census Worker
dialogue.line: Okay, I'll speak louder.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: No wait, turn left at the next intersection, then take the second right.

jokes.text: Get me a drill, screws, bulletin board? — 'No, I cannot.' — Okay, I tried. Bye.
jokes.setup: Hickey approaches the janitor to get materials to hang the bulletin board
jokes.punchline: His entire attempt is a one-sentence request followed by instant surrender — 'Okay, I tried. Bye.' — a parody of institutional passivity
jokes.explanation: Hickey's 'Okay, I tried. Bye.' is a great character beat — a former cop who has completely given up on systems. The joke is in the speed of his surrender and the total absence of persistence. Very character-integrated.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: What if we just killed him?

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: We're not killing anyone, Chang.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: I'm just saying, it's on the table.

jokes.text: If you wanna hang a bulletin board, get a work order. — 'They're more powerful than you?'
jokes.setup: Janitor explains bureaucratic procedure
jokes.punchline: Hickey's flat question — 'They're more powerful than you?' — reframes bureaucratic process as a power hierarchy, which is both absurdist and accurate
jokes.explanation: Hickey's cop-brain reducing organizational process to pure dominance hierarchy is a sharp, economical character observation. Sets up the bureaucratic labyrinth theme.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Hi Professor Pushpin!

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Have you seen Crazy Schmidt around?

jokes.text: I can't hear either. — 'Are you deaf? But you read lips?' — Gibberish. You're good.
jokes.setup: Abed is on census duty; he encounters a hearing-impaired woman and admits he can't hear either (he's wearing earbuds or similar)
jokes.punchline: The exchange of miscommunication culminates in Abed evaluating her lip-reading of his presumably unintelligible speech as 'Gibberish. You're good.' — a perverse compliment
jokes.explanation: Unusual comedic beat — the compliment 'Gibberish. You're good.' reframes incompetence as a test she passed. Abed's clinical evaluation of human interaction is well-deployed here.

dialogue.speaker: Janitor
dialogue.line: I'll get to it. I got a work order from 1987 I haven't even started yet.

jokes.text: I wish I knew sign language. — 'I detonated a mollusc.'
jokes.setup: Abed expresses a wish to communicate in sign language with the woman
jokes.punchline: She signs something; the subtitle reveals it as 'I detonated a mollusc' — suggesting either a catastrophic mistranslation or an utterly bizarre non-sequitur
jokes.explanation: Genuinely surprising and strange. 'I detonated a mollusc' is comedy-writing gold precisely because it's so specific and so wrong — it's either a subtitle gag (the closed captioning is wrong) or a pure non-sequitur. Either way, the specificity of 'mollusc' rather than any other animal elevates it. High originality.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Let's see... priority one: fix the copier. Priority two: replace the broken pencil sharpener. Priority three...

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Oh wow, this one's from 1987. 'Repair the east wing foundation.' Still in the queue.

jokes.text: Are you gonna have another intense burst of compatibility with a girl we never see again?
jokes.setup: Abed is having a surprisingly deep connection with the hearing-impaired woman
jokes.punchline: Britta calls out the sitcom trope directly — the one-episode love interest who disappears — breaking the fourth wall while remaining in character
jokes.explanation: Classic Community meta-commentary done well. Britta identifying the sitcom convention of episodic romantic interests — 'a girl we never see again' — is both a genuine character observation (Abed's pattern) and a show-aware joke. It's earned because Abed actually does this repeatedly in the series. The phrasing 'intense burst of compatibility' is particularly precise. This is Community at its most self-aware. Comparable to the 8.0 anchor.

dialogue.speaker: Hickey
dialogue.line: You think you can get this board hung?

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Please. I've hung plenty of things. I once organized an entire linen closet by thread count.

dialogue.speaker: Hickey
dialogue.line: That's not the same thing.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Oh, I'm sorry, did you need it done, or did you need it done *perfectly*? Because I can do both. In fact, I'll have it up before lunch, and it'll be so level, so perfectly centered, that you'll weep. You'll actually weep at the beauty of this board's placement.

jokes.text: The midterm dance will need a visual theme, like 'Let's Blow Off Steam,' and it's trains.
jokes.setup: Discussion of what theme the dance should have
jokes.punchline: Duncan pitches a theme that IS an explanation — 'Let's Blow Off Steam' — immediately deflated by confirming it's literally just trains
jokes.explanation: Duncan's literal interpretation of the pun as a sufficient decoration theme is funny in its bored pragmatism. Sets up the dance-theme runner nicely.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Oh wow, is that a wood burnt sign? That's so cool! You know, I've actually been researching all the different departments here at Greendale and their inter-departmental relationships. It's great for networking.

jokes.text: I have an idea. — 'Your last idea was to murder.'
jokes.setup: Chang volunteers an idea for the dance theme
jokes.punchline: Duncan matter-of-factly recalls that Chang's previous idea was murder — delivered as a mundane historical fact
jokes.explanation: Perfect economy and character integration. Duncan's flat delivery of 'your last idea was to murder' treats Chang's history of villainy as an ordinary logistical concern. The casualness is everything. Very Community — dark backstory used as a mundane punchline.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: This is the most beautifully engineered toilet I've ever seen. The porcelain glaze, the water pressure, the way it handles... heavy loads.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: I think this is the beginning of a beautiful friendship.

jokes.text: I have a lifetime of experience with red tape. I know when to walk away. — 'Yeah, you do.' — The system is lazy. I have integrity, too much to deal with any of it.
jokes.setup: Hickey has failed to get the work order moving and is philosophically surrendering
jokes.punchline: He frames his capitulation as a virtue — 'too much integrity to deal with it' — which is exactly backwards. Annie's 'Yeah, you do' is the perfect dry acknowledgment.
jokes.explanation: Hickey rationalizing defeat as moral superiority is a sharp character note — the cynical ex-cop who's reframed burnout as wisdom. Annie's one-line response ('Yeah, you do') is acidic without being hostile.

dialogue.speaker: Bob Waite
dialogue.line: You know, running this place is like running a meat processing plant. You got your quality control, your waste management, your union issues...

dialogue.speaker: Bob Waite
dialogue.line: And at the end of the day, somebody's gotta make the hard decisions about who stays and who gets ground up into sausage.

jokes.text: Oh, Professor Pushpin. Jerry, Carlo, Crazy Schmidt. I'm Annie. — 'You learned our names.' — Crazy Schmidt, how are C.J.'s clarinet lessons going?
jokes.setup: Annie approaches the janitors by name, demonstrating her signature overachieving people skills
jokes.punchline: She knows intimate personal details — the nickname 'Crazy Schmidt,' C.J.'s clarinet lessons — which both impresses and reveals her calculating social strategy
jokes.explanation: Annie's manipulation-via-warmth is a great character beat. Using the nickname 'Crazy Schmidt' unselfconsciously, then pivoting to hyper-specific personal knowledge, perfectly captures her 'type A who weaponizes care' characterization. The janitors' stunned 'you learned our names' is the tell.

dialogue.speaker: Hickey
dialogue.line: So you're telling me we go through all that paperwork, all those forms, all those signatures, just to trade porn for bulletin board?

jokes.text: There you go. That should happen in three to six business months.
jokes.setup: Annie successfully charms the janitor into submitting a work order
jokes.punchline: The timeframe revealed is 'three to six business months' — not days, not weeks, months — delivered as a perfectly normal estimate
jokes.explanation: 'Three to six business months' is a great absurdist escalation of the standard 'three to five business days' cliché. The specificity of 'business months' — implying non-business months also exist — is the elegant twist that makes it land.

dialogue.speaker: Hickey
dialogue.line: You see, kid, in this world you gotta learn how things really work. It's all about who you know, not what you know.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: But Mr. Hickey, that doesn't seem right. Shouldn't merit and hard work matter?

dialogue.speaker: Hickey
dialogue.line: That's what they want you to think. It's like that movie, Labyrinth. You gotta navigate the maze, make deals with the goblin king.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: I thought in Labyrinth, Sarah defeats the Goblin King by believing in herself and her friends?

dialogue.speaker: Hickey
dialogue.line: Yeah, well, that's the Disney version. In real bureaucracy, you just pay the goblin king and move on.

jokes.text: Any way we could bump that up a little so it's somewhere above 'Lower flag for Reagan's death'?
jokes.setup: The work order is at the bottom of the queue; Annie wants it prioritized
jokes.punchline: Her reference point for 'above' is a Reagan funeral flag directive — implying the queue hasn't been touched since at least 2004
jokes.explanation: Sharp joke that works on two levels: institutional decay (the queue hasn't been worked in a decade) and a specific Reagan reference that grounds the absurdity historically. 'Somewhere above Reagan's death' is an inspired specificity.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Bulletin boards are essential! They post missing persons, community events, important announcements...

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Annie, no one reads those.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: They do! People need them for housing, jobs, selling items...

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: She's right. I found my apartment on a bulletin board.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Exactly! And bands use them to find musicians. Bad bands need bad bass players!

jokes.text: We were just starting to like you.
jokes.setup: Annie asks what the difference is between janitors and custodians (implying there is none)
jokes.punchline: The janitors' affection for Annie, just established, is immediately withdrawn by her gaffe — 'we were just starting to like you' delivered as a flat warning
jokes.explanation: Good comic beat — the janitor/custodian distinction is absurd but the wounded delivery makes it funny. The speed of the reversal (from charmed to offended) is the joke.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: This bulletin board is not just cork and wood—it's a canvas for community expression! Every pushpin is a voice, every posted flyer a testament to our collective spirit!

jokes.text: Sandals! Sandals!
jokes.setup: Annie is trying to pursue a custodian through what appears to be a wet floor or some obstruction
jokes.punchline: The only thing we hear is Annie frantically calling out 'Sandals! Sandals!' — implying she's slipping, running, or reacting to some physical hazard in inappropriate footwear
jokes.explanation: The ambiguity of 'Sandals! Sandals!' is itself the joke — we don't know exactly what's happening but the word repeated with urgency implies Annie's overachieving physicality has been defeated by footwear. Works as pure physical comedy inference.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: My theme is 'Cowboy Spaceman Detective,' a perfect blend of genres that transcends traditional categorization.

jokes.text: Sorry, this is a closed function. We don't discuss business at mixers.
jokes.setup: Annie tries to do business at the custodians' mixer party
jokes.punchline: The custodians have social protocols identical to corporate networking events — 'closed function,' 'we don't discuss business at mixers' — treating a school janitor gathering as a formal professional occasion
jokes.explanation: The custodians mirroring corporate culture is the episode's central satirical joke, and this is its first full articulation. The gap between their status and their self-important protocols is reliably funny.

jokes.text: Get a load of that wood burnt sign. Did Mr. Whitney in Woodshop make that for you guys?
jokes.setup: Hickey and Annie are trying to work the custodian mixer
jokes.punchline: Hickey immediately deploys a sycophantic compliment about their hand-crafted sign — but it's slightly condescending in its specificity (naming the woodshop teacher who made it for them)
jokes.explanation: Hickey's cop-instinct to work a room by flattering the sign — with the deflating detail that a woodshop teacher made it — is a good character note. The specificity grounds it.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: Why are you crying?

dialogue.speaker: Other Character
dialogue.line: I'm not crying, you're crying!

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: No, I'm not... *touches face* Oh my God, I am crying.

jokes.text: Flushes like a DC-10 turbine. Probably exceeds code. But what's wrong with a little friendship between departments?
jokes.setup: Hickey is buttering up the custodians at their mixer by complimenting their bathroom toilet
jokes.punchline: He delivers a weirdly technical toilet compliment ('DC-10 turbine,' 'exceeds code') then pivots to 'friendship between departments' — the juxtaposition of toilet enthusiasm with diplomatic language
jokes.explanation: Hickey's bribery strategy — leading with toilet appreciation as a diplomatic overture — is very funny. 'Flushes like a DC-10 turbine' is specific in the way good comedy writing requires. The pivot to 'friendship between departments' is perfect deadpan.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: You know what? I'm tired of being treated like I don't matter. I've given everything to this school, and nobody respects me. Nobody listens to me.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: But that's okay. I know why. It's because I'm Asian.

jokes.text: It's election time. If I don't break out sausages, my ass goes in the grinder next January.
jokes.setup: Bob is explaining why he's throwing a generous party for his custodians
jokes.punchline: The sausage/grinder metaphor accidentally (or intentionally) puts him in the sausage, completing the implicit threat. The vulgarity of 'my ass goes in the grinder' is both literal (sausage grinder) and figurative (political destruction).
jokes.explanation: Good political satire compressed into a single mixed metaphor. The custodian union-boss as a politician managing constituents is the satirical frame, and this line captures it economically.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: You guys don't understand! You've all abandoned me! First you didn't invite me to the study group, then you excluded me from the paintball game, and now—now you're telling me I can't be the dean anymore!

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: And you know what this is really about? You don't think I'm qualified. You think I'm too unstable, too unpredictable!

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: Well, let me tell you something—this is discrimination! This is about my background! This is about where I come from!

jokes.text: They want their porn unblocked. — 'Then they'll give you your board.' — 'That's what that was?'
jokes.setup: Bob has been elaborately showing them a web filter problem as a coded bribe request
jokes.punchline: Hickey cuts straight to 'they want their porn unblocked' after Bob's elaborate runaround. Annie's 'that's what that was?' reveals she missed the implication entirely.
jokes.explanation: Good two-beat joke: Hickey's blunt translation of the custodian boss's euphemistic dance, then Annie's naïve retrospective confusion. The contrast between Hickey's world-weariness and Annie's obliviousness is character-perfect.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Look, I need complete access to all the restricted websites. Porn, gambling, everything.

dialogue.speaker: IT Person
dialogue.line: Um... okay? That's... that's a pretty big request.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: I don't care. I need it. Full access, no blocks, no filters.

dialogue.speaker: IT Person
dialogue.line: Can I ask what this is for?

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Research. Now are you going to help me or do I need to go to Dean Pelton?

jokes.text: How did you know? Did you investigate pornography when you were a cop?
jokes.setup: Hickey immediately understood the pornography bribe; Annie is baffled by his instinct
jokes.punchline: Annie's question — asking if Hickey investigated pornography as a cop — is delivered with earnest curiosity, unaware of how it sounds
jokes.explanation: Annie's earnestness making the question inadvertently comic is a solid character beat. Hickey's 'something like that' non-answer is appropriately dry.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: I've decorated the gym with authentic bear-themed decorations for the midterm dance.

dialogue.speaker: Duncan
dialogue.line: Chang, why is there a birthday cake and party streamers mixed in with the bear motif?

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: Because bears have birthdays too, Duncan. It's called diversity.

jokes.text: Welcome to the labyrinth. Only there ain't no puppets or bisexual rock stars down here.
jokes.setup: Annie and Hickey have just discovered the full depth of bureaucratic corruption
jokes.punchline: Hickey references the film Labyrinth (with David Bowie), noting their version lacks both puppets AND the bisexual rock star, grounding the absurdity in pop culture with an unexpected candor about Bowie's sexuality
jokes.explanation: Hickey's Labyrinth reference works on multiple levels: thematic (bureaucratic maze), pop culture, and the casual aside about Bowie's sexuality as a distinguishing feature. 'Bisexual rock star' is both a precise character description and completely unexpected from this character. High quotability and genuine wit.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: Now listen, we need to carve out some time in the budget for this initiative.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Dean, we're not stuffing this turkey until we know what we're working with.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: But if we don't baste the numbers now, the whole thing will dry out by Q4.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: You realize you're mixing your metaphors here, right?

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: Am I? Because I'm pretty sure we're both gravy-deep in this commitment.

jokes.text: So at the centre of it all, if you're lucky, a piece of cork and a few pins. So, what, is it worth it?
jokes.setup: Hickey is philosophically framing the absurdity of the bureaucratic quest for a bulletin board
jokes.punchline: He reduces the entire labyrinth to its endpoint: 'a piece of cork' — questioning Annie's idealism with his own nihilism
jokes.explanation: This is where the episode's thematic joke lives — the entire A-plot is a Sisyphean quest for a piece of cork. Hickey's dry articulation of this sets up Annie's idealistic speech. The joke is in the deflation, and it's character-perfect for Hickey.

dialogue.speaker: Parking Guy
dialogue.line: You see, I have the power to boot cars. I also have the power to un-boot cars. Some would say that makes me a god.

dialogue.speaker: Parking Guy
dialogue.line: Annie, your father never gave you positive reinforcement, so you seek it from authority figures. That's why you're so eager to please me.

jokes.text: Is that all a bulletin board is? A piece of cork? ...people whose bad bands need bad bass players. To them, every pushpin has the power to change the future.
jokes.setup: Hickey has dismissed the bulletin board as just cork and pins
jokes.punchline: Annie's passionate defense of community bulletin boards culminates in the absurd specificity of 'bad bands need bad bass players' — the deflating example in an otherwise earnest speech
jokes.explanation: The speech earns its comedy from Annie's completely sincere delivery of increasingly grandiose claims, punctuated by the absurd specificity of 'bad bands need bad bass players.' The specificity (not just bands — bad bands; not just players — bad players) shows real writing craft.

dialogue.speaker: Waldron
dialogue.line: Look, we need to carve out a deal here before things get too heated.

dialogue.speaker: Waldron
dialogue.line: I'm not trying to stuff this turkey of a negotiation, but we're running out of gravy on the clock.

dialogue.speaker: Waldron
dialogue.line: So either we can have our pie and eat it too, or this whole cornucopia of dreams just gets cold and goes back in the oven.

jokes.text: I learned how to say this in sign language. [signs something] — 'You're a fast learner.' — I learned how to say this in sign language. — 'Don't forget I can read lips.' — I learned how to say this in sign language.
jokes.setup: Abed wants to communicate with the woman in sign language
jokes.punchline: He keeps signing 'I learned how to say this in sign language' — a recursive loop where the CONTENT of what he learned is the sentence about learning it. Three repetitions escalate into absurdism.
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's best joke. The recursive logic — Abed has learned to sign exactly the sentence 'I learned how to say this in sign language,' making his only signed communication a tautology — is philosophically absurd and structurally perfect. The three-beat escalation, the woman's charmed response ('you're a fast learner'), then her warning ('don't forget I can read lips') building to the third repetition is flawlessly constructed. This is Community at peak Abed — using his literal-minded character to generate a genuinely recursive joke. This approaches the top anchor territory.

dialogue.speaker: Waldron
dialogue.line: You see, in dinosaur times, there was an abundance of resources. No bureaucracy, no parking department to regulate where you could leave your Brachiosaurus.

jokes.text: Bear Down For Midterms.
jokes.setup: Chang pitches his dance theme idea with great excitement
jokes.punchline: The theme is 'Bear Down For Midterms' — a pun on 'bear down' (concentrate/work hard) that is both obvious and, in retrospect, foreshadows the bear mauling disaster
jokes.explanation: In isolation a mild pun joke; retroactively becomes much funnier when we learn Chang was inspired by a real bear mauling. The rewatch value is high because it recontextualizes the entire scene.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: That's right. Solar power, wind power, and of course, the power of a father's approval — which, let's be honest, you're never going to get, Waldron.

jokes.text: You can't just repeat it. You need to explain yourself.
jokes.setup: Chang says 'Bear Down For Midterms' and then repeats it when met with confusion
jokes.punchline: Duncan's objection is hilariously reasonable — repeating a confusing phrase more forcefully is not an explanation
jokes.explanation: Good comic beat — Duncan identifying the communication failure of repetition-as-explanation is a recognizable social observation. Functions well in the rhythm of the Chang/Bear sequence.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: I'm going to talk turkey with you.

dialogue.speaker: Waldron
dialogue.line: Oh, you're actually going to talk like a turkey?

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: Gobble gobble gobble gobble!

jokes.text: 'Fly On The Wall For Midterms,' you might ask, 'What do you mean?'
jokes.setup: Jeff is explaining why 'Bear Down' as a pun doesn't automatically make sense as a theme
jokes.punchline: He constructs a parallel absurd pun ('Fly on the Wall for Midterms') to illustrate that puns don't translate to themes by themselves
jokes.explanation: Jeff's rhetorical construction of a parallel bad pitch is good writing — it both makes his logical point and is itself funny. 'Fly On The Wall For Midterms' is funny because it immediately sounds like something that would be greenlit at Greendale.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Why are there bear decorations everywhere?

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: There was a bear attack this morning.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Wait, an actual bear attack? Not a drill?

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: Very much an actual bear. We're processing it as a campus community.

jokes.text: Chang? Are you crying? ... I don't know if you guys see me as human anymore. I don't know if it's like a joke to you. Are all Asian men like a joke?
jokes.setup: The group dismisses Chang's theme idea; he becomes increasingly emotional
jokes.punchline: Chang's existential breakdown over a dance theme — escalating from professional hurt to racial identity crisis — is simultaneously cringe, character comedy, and a sly satire of his own history of manipulation
jokes.explanation: Chang weaponizing race to deflect from a reasonable critique of his theme idea is both funny and uncomfortable — classic Community cringe. The escalation from hurt feelings to 'are all Asian men a joke?' is audacious. It's saved from being offensive by the implicit understanding that Chang is manipulating them, which the audience knows.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: The bear is our school mascot. It's a symbol of strength and pride.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff Winger
dialogue.line: Yeah, except there's been a bear attack in the area. Three hikers mauled just yesterday.

dialogue.speaker: Britta Perry
dialogue.line: So we're literally celebrating the exact thing that just murdered people.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: Well, when you put it that way, it sounds bad.

jokes.text: Chang, what can we do here? — 'Bear Down For Midterms.' — Okay. / Okay, well... We'll put up some bear things? We'll bear down. For midterms.
jokes.setup: Jeff tries to appease the crying Chang by asking what they can do
jokes.punchline: Chang's demand — after all that — is simply to have his original idea accepted. Jeff and Duncan's confused, defeated capitulation ('We'll bear down. For midterms.') is the kicker.
jokes.explanation: The payoff to Chang's manipulation is that he just... wanted his idea accepted. The group's resigned 'we'll bear down. For midterms.' is a perfect deflation of the entire emotional escalation. 'We'll bear down. For midterms.' delivered with zero enthusiasm is a quotable, character-rich moment.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: Oh no. Oh no no no. I just realized... I didn't come up with the bear idea. I saw it on the news. Some guy actually did that. I subconsciously plagiarized from a real tragedy.

jokes.text: If the filter is mistakenly blocking a site, they just need to submit the URL and I can— 'Okay. What do you want?' — 'Excuse me?' — 'Tell us what we can do, so that you can do this for us.' — 'Oh, cool. I didn't know it could work that way.'
jokes.setup: Annie and Hickey are asking the IT woman to unblock sites for the custodians as a bribe
jokes.punchline: The IT woman begins explaining proper procedure; Hickey bluntly cuts to 'What do you want?' The IT woman's response — 'Oh, cool, I didn't know it could work that way' — reveals her genuine ignorance of bribery as a transaction
jokes.explanation: The IT woman's naïve delight at discovering bribery as a system ('Oh, cool, I didn't know it could work that way') is a great inversion — she's not corrupt, she's just never been offered a quid pro quo before. Her enthusiasm for the concept is funnier than cynicism would be.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: I'm about to sign this form, but I noticed you wrote 'assorted pickles' instead of 'mixed pickles.'

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: They're the same thing, Dean.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: No, they're not. And until you change it, this form doesn't get signed.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: You're holding up the entire budget over pickles?

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: I'm holding up this budget until I get some respect around here. And respect starts with proper pickle nomenclature.

jokes.text: Let's be clear. I want everything to get through that blocker. — 'What do you mean everything?' — 'Everything!'
jokes.setup: Annie thinks she's negotiating a targeted URL unblock
jokes.punchline: The IT woman reveals she wants ALL content unblocked — she's going full corruption — and her emphatic 'Everything!' shows she's fully committed to this bribe lifestyle she just discovered
jokes.explanation: The escalation from 'targeted unblock' to 'EVERYTHING' in about 20 seconds is a sharp joke about how quickly institutional corruption scales once it starts. The IT woman's radicalization into full corruption is a micro-arc.

dialogue.speaker: Hickey
dialogue.line: Annie, I'm disappointed in you. You've become everything I despise - corrupt, dishonest, willing to compromise your principles for personal gain.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: That's not fair, Hickey. You don't understand the situation.

dialogue.speaker: Hickey
dialogue.line: Oh, I understand perfectly. And you know what the worst part is? I thought you were better than this.

jokes.text: I'm very happy right now.
jokes.setup: The deal has been struck — she gets parking, they get the board
jokes.punchline: Her flat, sincere declaration of happiness after getting what she wanted from her first-ever successful bribe
jokes.explanation: Four words, maximum economy. The IT woman's simple joy is funnier than any elaborate expression would be. Functions as a capper to her corruption arc.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: You can't just take down the bulletin board! It's a public space!

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: Actually, Jeff, as Dean, I have every right to remove it. The postings have become... problematic.

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: This is about censorship! We're living in a fascist state!

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Guys, we're talking about a bulletin board, not the fall of democracy.

jokes.text: So just, bears everywhere? — 'Yep.' — And then we'll have some cakes, party hats. Birthday stuff. This is coming together better than I thought.
jokes.setup: The group is planning the bear-themed dance
jokes.punchline: Chang adds 'birthday stuff' — cakes, party hats — which has nothing to do with midterms or bears, and Duncan just accepts it. The plan is incoherent but everyone is at peace with it.
jokes.explanation: Chang's random birthday additions to the bear theme are mildly funny — the group's resignation to incoherence is the joke. Light, functional.

jokes.text: Always had a passion for bulletins.
jokes.setup: Waldron from Parking is explaining why he wants control of all bulletin boards
jokes.punchline: His cover story — 'passion for bulletins' — is transparently pretextual, delivered with practiced sincerity
jokes.explanation: The absurdity of a 'passion for bulletins' as a character trait is mild but functional. Sets up the Parking power exposition.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: A fat dog is when you take two hot dogs and stack them on top of each other. Bah!

jokes.text: There was plenty of space to park in dinosaur times, but not one single Parking Department.
jokes.setup: Waldron is explaining the source of his department's power
jokes.punchline: He makes a logical argument about scarcity using dinosaurs — not as a metaphor but as a literal historical data point, implying the Parking Department is as old a concept as scarcity itself
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's sharpest lines. The philosophical argument that parking spaces aren't scarce in themselves — only the DEPARTMENT creates scarcity — is a genuine insight delivered via the absurd dinosaur example. 'Plenty of space to park in dinosaur times, but not one Parking Department' is excellent comedy writing: it's both a logical argument and completely insane. The specificity of dinosaur times grounds the absurdity. High quotability, high originality. Comfortably above the 8.0 anchor.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff Winger
dialogue.line: It's a real word. I read it on Wikipedia.

dialogue.speaker: Britta Perry
dialogue.line: Jeff, you can't just believe everything on Wikipedia.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff Winger
dialogue.line: Well, it's more reliable than you are.

jokes.text: You wanna control all bulletin boards in the school. Why? / You might wanna start talking turkey, Waldron, the Macy's Parade is almost over and Grandma's getting drunk.
jokes.setup: Hickey is trying to pressure Waldron into stating his actual demands
jokes.punchline: His threat/metaphor — 'the Macy's Parade is almost over and Grandma's getting drunk' — is so bizarre, colorful, and oddly specific that it functions as both a threat and a Hickey character reveal
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best lines and among the best in the season. 'The Macy's Parade is almost over and Grandma's getting drunk' is Hickey in full — he uses a homespun idiom that sounds like it means something, but its precise meaning is completely obscure. The specificity (Macy's Parade, not just 'parade'; Grandma, not just 'someone') creates a weirdly specific domestic image of dysfunction. It's also a perfect negotiation threat: intimidating through sheer inscrutability. This is the kind of line Community writes that no other show would, and it's entirely character-specific to Hickey.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: What if instead of a bear mascot, we had a Mantis Toboggan? It's a real thing. Look it up.

jokes.text: just like your dad's comes from a lack of hugs.
jokes.setup: Waldron has explained that his power comes from manufactured scarcity
jokes.punchline: He extends the metaphor to Hickey's father and 'a lack of hugs' — an unexpected psychoanalytic pivot delivered mid-argument
jokes.explanation: The pivot from institutional theory to 'your dad's power comes from lack of hugs' is a sharp insult structured as a logical parallel. It's genuinely surprising mid-monologue. Good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Bear down for midterms!

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Jeff, did you not hear about the bear attack?

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: What? No, I just... I mean, it's a saying.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: A saying that's deeply insensitive right now.

jokes.text: And you know what takes my power away? Carpools. Carpools organised through rideshares. Rideshares posted on bulletin boards, you son of—
jokes.setup: Waldron has established that scarcity is his power source
jokes.punchline: The cascade from carpools → rideshares → bulletin boards reveals his actual motivation — bulletin boards are his existential threat — and the revelation is so perfectly bureaucratic it tips into absurdism. The interrupted expletive is the button.
jokes.explanation: The logical chain is the joke: Parking → scarcity → carpools → rideshares → bulletin boards. The escalation is structurally impeccable — each step is causal and absurd. The realization that a Parking Director has been plotting against bulletin boards for existential reasons is a perfect Community joke about institutional logic taken to extremes. The interrupted 'you son of—' is a great button. This matches the 8.0 anchor benchmark.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: I'm not being deceptive. I'm providing employment for an interpreter.

jokes.text: Take the books off your head, we're done posturing.
jokes.setup: Waldron has been in full antagonist mode during his monologue
jokes.punchline: Hickey deflates the entire scene with 'take the books off your head' — implying Waldron has been physically posturing with books on his head, like a Dickensian villain — while simultaneously dismissing the whole performance
jokes.explanation: The visual of Waldron delivering his grandiose parking monologue with books balanced on his head is a perfect absurdist image. Hickey's flat 'we're done posturing' treats the entire operatic display as tiresome theater. Great comic economy.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: It's the Fat Dog Dance. It's a real thing.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: I've never heard of it.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: That's because you're not from the streets.

jokes.text: You want me to talk turkey, well, gobble, gobble... I want rideshares gone.
jokes.setup: Hickey tells Waldron to 'talk turkey'
jokes.punchline: Waldron takes the idiom literally, says 'gobble, gobble' and then states his actual demand — it's both a literal enactment of the idiom and a power move
jokes.explanation: The 'gobble, gobble' literalization of a common idiom is a small but precise joke — the character demonstrates the idiom rather than just fulfilling it. Very quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Singer
dialogue.line: Fat dog dance, fat dog dance, it's a real thing, fat dog dance. Fat dog dance, fat dog dance, look it up, it's in the dance, fat dog dance.

jokes.text: So you don't even know what Ewoks sound like? — 'The subtitles describe it as yip-chaa.' — 'That's actually pretty close.'
jokes.setup: Britta and Abed are doing census work; apparently discussing Star Wars
jokes.punchline: Abed has been getting his Ewok knowledge from closed captions rather than audio — 'yip-chaa' — and Britta confirms this is approximately accurate, suggesting she DOES know what Ewoks sound like despite everything
jokes.explanation: The joke has layers: Abed relies on subtitles (connecting to his literal communication style), 'yip-chaa' is a genuinely funny attempt to transcribe Ewok sounds, and Britta's authoritative confirmation ('actually pretty close') reveals her own nerd knowledge. The scene also quietly suggests Britta and Abed's beef has thawed, making the character work functional too.

dialogue.speaker: Unknown
dialogue.line: Wait, is that a fat dog dance?

dialogue.speaker: Unknown
dialogue.line: No, that's a bear.

jokes.text: I must say, I don't know what we did, but we sure did it.
jokes.setup: The dance is coming together despite nobody having a coherent plan
jokes.punchline: Duncan's self-congratulatory summary of their work — 'I don't know what we did, but we sure did it' — is both honest incomprehension and false pride
jokes.explanation: Very quotable, very Duncan. The sentence is constructed so the first clause ('I don't know what we did') and second clause ('but we sure did it') are logically incompatible, which is itself the joke. High economy, strong character integration for Duncan's particular brand of confident uselessness.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: Wait, what did I do? What protocol is this?

dialogue.speaker: Voice
dialogue.line: Self-destruct sequence initiated.

dialogue.speaker: Chang
dialogue.line: No, no, no! I just wanted to check my email!

jokes.text: After this morning in Wisconsin? Bear breaks loose at kid's party, mauls a bunch of people.
jokes.setup: Chang says the bear decor is 'too soon'; Jeff and Duncan have no idea what he means
jokes.punchline: Chang reveals the context: a bear mauled people at a child's party in Wisconsin that morning — which is both horrifying and absurd as a news event
jokes.explanation: The reveal that Chang's bear theme was inspired by an actual bear mauling he saw on the news (and then 'forgot' he saw) is a great dark comedy escalation. The specificity of Wisconsin, kids' party, and the casual 'mauls a bunch of people' delivery makes it land hard.

dialogue.speaker: Phone System
dialogue.line: Welcome to Greendale Community College. Press 1 for English.

dialogue.speaker: Phone System
dialogue.line: For Admissions, press 2. For Financial Aid, press 3. For a complex military operation to select a color, press 4.

dialogue.speaker: Phone System
dialogue.line: You have selected color selection. This is Operation Chromatic Shield. Please state your preferred hue using military phonetic alphabet. Bravo for Blue. Delta for... a different blue.

dialogue.speaker: Phone System
dialogue.line: Confirm your selection by entering the launch codes. We are now at DEFCON 2.

jokes.text: That's where I got the idea. Sometimes you hear something, forget you heard it, but you think you came up with... Oh, man, this is bad.
jokes.setup: Chang realizes he subconsciously plagiarized his theme from a traumatic news event
jokes.punchline: His half-articulated psychological explanation of cryptomnesia followed by 'Oh, man, this is bad' — the dawning awareness is funnier than the explanation
jokes.explanation: The cryptomnesia explanation — Chang accidentally ripping off a tragedy for a party theme — is psychologically specific and funny. His incomplete articulation of the concept ('sometimes you hear something...') mirrors the actual psychological state.

jokes.text: 'An Office of Bulletin Board Oversight.' What a novel idea. I'm gonna fill out this form right away. But first, a toast... to hanging a bulletin board. Easy-peasy, lemon squeezy.
jokes.setup: Annie and Hickey have negotiated through layers of bureaucracy to get the board hung
jokes.punchline: Waldron's triumphant toast — 'Easy-peasy, lemon squeezy' — is completely incongruous with the elaborate corrupt deal just concluded, delivered with sincere cheerfulness
jokes.explanation: The gap between the complexity of what just happened and 'easy-peasy, lemon squeezy' is the joke. The phrase is also a character note — this guy is genuinely unbothered by the corruption because it's just business to him.

jokes.text: First time toasting? Get in here, buddy. Easy-peasy, lemon squeezy. — 'I'm not saying that.'
jokes.setup: Waldron tries to get Hickey to join in his 'easy-peasy lemon squeezy' toast
jokes.punchline: Hickey flatly refuses: 'I'm not saying that.' — a brief assertion of dignity amid the corruption
jokes.explanation: Four words, maximum Hickey. His refusal to say the childish phrase is his only remaining dignity after everything that's happened. The joke is in the economy — no explanation, just 'I'm not saying that.'

jokes.text: Oh, well, I hate to be that guy, but I'm not signing this form until Professor Hickey says 'Easy-peasy, lemon squeezy.'
jokes.setup: Hickey has refused to say the phrase; Waldron needs to sign the form
jokes.punchline: Waldron makes saying the childish phrase a non-negotiable condition of the deal — the final, pettiest demand in a chain of corrupt negotiations
jokes.explanation: The final escalation of the bureaucratic absurdism — after porn, parking, and board oversight, the last demand is simply that a grumpy ex-cop say a childish phrase. This is structurally perfect: the pettiness of the final ask makes everything that preceded it even more absurd. Great payoff.

jokes.text: Annie Edison doesn't get nothing done. — 'Where should I put that bulletin? On a sham piece of cork controlled by a Parking guy that lights his cigars on student rideshares?'
jokes.setup: Annie delivers an impassioned speech about not being stopped by the system
jokes.punchline: Hickey's immediate deflation — where exactly should she post her victory bulletin? On the corrupted board she just created? — is the perfect ironic undercut
jokes.explanation: Hickey's 'where should I put that bulletin?' is a devastating structural callback — Annie's victory bulletin would go on the very board whose existence now represents corruption. 'A parking guy that lights his cigars on student rideshares' is vivid, specific, and perfectly summarizes the episode's satirical argument. This is Hickey's best moment — the cynical mentor fully articulating the lesson. Among the episode's strongest lines.

jokes.text: Oh, man, this got Sorkin-y.
jokes.setup: Hickey has delivered an impassioned, morally complex speech about institutional corruption and Annie's complicity
jokes.punchline: Jeff breaks the tension by naming the tonal register — 'this got Sorkin-y' — referencing Aaron Sorkin's signature earnest, rapid-fire moral speechifying
jokes.explanation: Perfect meta-commentary. 'This got Sorkin-y' names the exact dramatic register the scene has entered — the earnest institutional-corruption speech, the moral awakening, the rapid-fire dialogue — and deflates it in one word. It's also very Jeff: he uses pop culture references to avoid genuine emotional engagement. The economy is exceptional — four words do the work of a paragraph. Very quotable, high rewatch value. This is Community's meta-commentary at its most precise.

jokes.text: Yeah, well, I didn't think anything in particular of you, and now I see why!
jokes.setup: Hickey says 'I thought better of you, young lady' — a condescending reprimand
jokes.punchline: Annie's comeback is that she hadn't thought anything of him specifically — which is both less insulting and more insulting
jokes.explanation: Annie's comeback is well-constructed — the inversion of Hickey's rhetorical form ('I thought better of you' → 'I didn't think anything of you') and the 'now I see why' kicker. Good Annie character work: her competitive instinct even in a moment of moral defeat.

jokes.text: Okay, I didn't follow most of that, but it feels like I ought to do this: [commits to something physically]
jokes.setup: An intense, Sorkin-esque argument has just occurred between Annie and Hickey
jokes.punchline: Duncan has not followed any of it but feels socially compelled to register a physical or verbal response — his oblivious reaction is the joke
jokes.explanation: Duncan's admission of complete incomprehension while still feeling obligated to perform a reaction is good character comedy — he's socially aware enough to know he should react, too oblivious to know why. The vagueness of 'do this' (we can't see what he does) makes it slightly weaker in transcript form.

jokes.text: 'Fat Dog For Midterms'? — 'Yeah.' — 'Pretty cool.' — 'I don't understand.' — 'That's an expression. Fat Dog For Midterms. Like, Don't sweat it. Fat dog it. Hang out, relax, like a fat dog.' — 'Look it up on Wikipedia. There's an entry in there.'
jokes.setup: Chang has replaced 'Bear Down For Midterms' with 'Fat Dog For Midterms' as the dance theme, implying it's a known expression
jokes.punchline: Chang's explanation of 'fat dog' as an established idiom — with the insistence that Wikipedia has an entry — is transparently a made-up expression being sold with confidence. 'Yep.' is the final button.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. 'Fat Dog For Midterms' is funny as a standalone phrase, but Chang's confident explanation — 'like a fat dog,' 'hang out, relax' — and the Wikipedia authority claim elevates it. The specificity of 'like a fat dog' (what does a fat dog do? exactly nothing) is perfect absurdist logic. 'Yep.' is an ideal deadpan confirmation. High originality, excellent structure, peak Chang character work. Easily above the 8.0 anchor.

jokes.text: Sometimes it feels like you don't take us seriously. We bring it on ourselves, but it's still pretty frustrating.
jokes.setup: Annie expresses skepticism about 'Fat Dog For Midterms'
jokes.punchline: Chang's rebuke — 'sometimes it feels like you don't take us seriously, we bring it on ourselves, but it's still frustrating' — is both a character admission and a meta-commentary on how the show treats its supporting characters
jokes.explanation: This is Chang's sharpest moment in the episode and possibly in this period of the series. 'We bring it on ourselves, but it's still pretty frustrating' is a perfect self-aware line — it acknowledges Chang's history of being ridiculous while also being a genuine complaint about being dismissed. It echoes his earlier breakdown but in a far more self-aware, economical form. The meta-layer (supporting characters who know they're not taken seriously) makes it particularly rich for Community. High character integration.

jokes.text: Annie, is this a race thing? — 'Race.' — 'No! God, no.'
jokes.setup: Annie is still skeptical of 'Fat Dog For Midterms'; Chang asks if it's racial
jokes.punchline: Jeff and Chang tag-team the race card again — a callback to Chang's earlier manipulation — and Annie's horrified denial is the punchline
jokes.explanation: The second use of the race card is a callback that works, but it's slightly less effective than the first — the element of surprise is gone. Still lands because Annie's response is proportional to the manipulation.

jokes.text: Just pick an idea and bear down on it. — 'Really poor choice of words, Ben. Too soon.'
jokes.setup: Jeff tells Annie to 'bear down' on a decision
jokes.punchline: Chang's immediate correction — 'really poor choice of words, Ben. Too soon.' — in the context of the Wisconsin bear mauling is a perfect callback
jokes.explanation: The callback to the bear mauling via the common idiom 'bear down' is structurally perfect — the phrase now carries a dark double meaning Chang is exquisitely sensitive to. 'Really poor choice of words, Ben. Too soon.' is very quotable. Great economy, great structure. The use of Jeff's first name ('Ben') adds a small additional character note.

jokes.text: You guys are right. I'm sorry. I've had a really hard day. I need to just fat dog this concept.
jokes.setup: Annie surrenders her skepticism about the Fat Dog theme
jokes.punchline: She uses 'fat dog' as a verb — 'fat dog this concept' — immediately adopting the made-up idiom in context, completing its integration into the group's vocabulary
jokes.explanation: Annie using 'fat dog' as a verb is the confirmation that the absurd phrase has been successfully laundered into the group's dialect. 'Fat dog this concept' is quotable and shows Annie's capitulation through linguistic assimilation. Good callback payoff.

jokes.text: But sometimes great days can turn ugly. Like when Queen Stevarios massacres the entire Vogadash family at Lord Brince's funeral in Bloodlines of Conquest. That's how the last book ends.
jokes.setup: Abed comments philosophically on the day
jokes.punchline: He delivers the ultimate Bloodlines of Conquest spoiler — the entire ending — using it as a metaphor for the day turning ugly, completing his revenge arc against Britta
jokes.explanation: The payoff to the episode's B-plot spoiler runner. Abed weaponizes the entire series finale as a 'philosophical' observation — the structure of using 'sometimes great days turn ugly' as a segue into the ultimate spoiler is perfect. The callback rewards viewers who've been tracking the thread since the opening scene. The specific detail of the massacre location ('Lord Brince's funeral') adds absurdist specificity.

jokes.text: Sugar. — 'Thank you.'
jokes.setup: Abed has just spoiled the entire series for Britta as revenge for her spoiling earlier
jokes.punchline: Britta's reaction to being devastated by the spoiler is simply 'Sugar' — a minced oath that beautifully underplays the moment — and Abed's 'Thank you' acknowledges the win without gloating
jokes.explanation: The deflation of Britta's reaction to 'Sugar' — a completely inadequate response to being spoiled — combined with Abed's gracious 'Thank you' (acknowledging the victory) is perfect economy. Two words do enormous work.

jokes.text: I'm sorry, Abed, but to the spoiler goes the victory. But I really liked her. She likes you too, but she also likes cash.
jokes.setup: Abed is devastated by the revelation about the character he liked
jokes.punchline: Britta's consolation — 'she likes you too, but she also likes cash' — is simultaneously emotionally hollow and weirdly practical
jokes.explanation: Britta's explanation of a fictional character's mercenary motivations as though they're a real person's flaws is a good Britta joke — she's simultaneously competitive and trying to be kind, and the result is tone-deaf.

jokes.text: Now I feel bad. But you learned a lesson, and I gave a differently-abled person a job.
jokes.setup: Abed is devastated; Britta is trying to find a silver lining
jokes.punchline: Britta's consolation spins her manipulation (using the hearing-impaired woman as a spoiler asset) as social progress — 'I gave a differently-abled person a job'
jokes.explanation: Peak Britta. She's genuinely trying to feel good about exploiting a deaf woman by reframing it as employment opportunity. 'I gave a differently-abled person a job' is the perfect Britta self-justification — progressive language deployed to cover selfish behavior. High character integration: this is ONLY a Britta line. Approaches the 8.0 anchor.

jokes.text: Oh, no. Now I really feel bad. Wait, no. Come back. Let's be fat dogs about this.
jokes.setup: Abed walks away; Britta tries to call him back
jokes.punchline: She deploys 'fat dogs' — the newly minted made-up idiom — as a genuine appeal for calm, confirming the phrase's absorption into the group
jokes.explanation: Britta saying 'let's be fat dogs about this' is the third deployment of the phrase and completes its lifecycle as a running gag. Each character's sincere use of the made-up idiom is funnier than the last.

jokes.text: Hello. What happened to you? — 'Nothing. You never called.' — 'I'm sorry. The year of the gas leak, but I won't use that as an excuse. I can be inconsiderate and a lot of other things.'
jokes.setup: Hickey runs into someone he apparently stood up
jokes.punchline: He explains his absence with 'the year of the gas leak' — a canonical Community in-joke about Season 4 (widely considered the weakest) being retroactively explained as a gas-leak-induced hallucination — then immediately undercuts his own excuse
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes for invested Community fans. 'The year of the gas leak' is a callback to the show's own self-deprecating canon — Season 4 was produced without Dan Harmon and widely disliked, then retroactively dismissed as a 'gas leak year.' Using it as a character's excuse for personal failings, then immediately saying 'but I won't use that as an excuse,' is a perfect meta-joke. The character integration is strong: Hickey is admitting real personal failings while the show simultaneously acknowledges its own. Very high quotability for fans.

jokes.text: Me too. I guess I could've put in some effort. — 'Do you want to go to lunch sometime?' — 'No. I'd like to go to dinner. Now.' — 'I can do that.' — 'I started this coat check without permission anyway.'
jokes.setup: Hickey and the woman have reconciled; she suggests lunch
jokes.punchline: She upgrades to dinner immediately ('No. I'd like to go to dinner. Now.') then adds the non-sequitur that she started the coat check without permission — implying casual institutional rebellion is her personal baseline
jokes.explanation: 'I started this coat check without permission anyway' is a great button — it establishes her character in one line and rhymes with the episode's bureaucratic theme. The dinner upgrade ('No. I'd like to go to dinner. Now.') is punchy and character-revealing.

jokes.text: Me too. I guess I could've put in some effort. / Do you want to go to lunch sometime? / No. I'd like to go to dinner. Now. / I can do that.
jokes.setup: Abed and the deaf girl have reconciled and he offers a low-key lunch invitation
jokes.punchline: She escalates — 'No. I'd like to go to dinner. Now.' — subverting his tentative offer with confident, immediate escalation; and his 'I can do that' is the perfect deadpan acceptance
jokes.explanation: Good subversion. Abed offering a small, non-committal lunch gets trumped by her directness. The escalation from 'lunch sometime' to 'dinner, now' is funny and also characterizes her well. The brief, complete 'I can do that' is satisfying.

jokes.text: I started this coat check without permission anyway.
jokes.setup: She's been running a coat check at the dance
jokes.punchline: In leaving for dinner, she casually reveals the coat check was entirely unsanctioned — a micro-hustle at the school dance, run on her own authority
jokes.explanation: Perfect character reveal in one throwaway line. She's been running a gray-market coat check and left it mid-service without warning — she's mercenary (consistent with accepting cash from Britta), entrepreneurial, and completely unconcerned about the abandoned coats. Great economy; the line does huge character work.

jokes.text: Excuse me. Excuse me. Excuse me. [prolonged sequence] No! No! All right, all right, enough! Let's go.
jokes.setup: Hickey and Annie are apparently trying to get through a crowd or navigate some obstacle at the dance
jokes.punchline: The repeated 'Excuse me' escalates to 'No!' — suggesting a physical confrontation or absurd obstacle — culminating in Hickey shutting it down with 'All right, all right, enough!'
jokes.explanation: Hard to fully evaluate without visuals — this appears to be a physical comedy sequence where the dialogue gives only minimal information. The escalation from polite 'excuse me' to full confrontation is a standard physical comedy arc. Scores lower due to being mostly inference.

jokes.text: There's a brand-new dance based on an old phrase / It's called The Fat Dog and it will amaze / You've heard this expression your entire life / It's not made up, it's not made up [dance song performed at the midterm dance]
jokes.setup: The midterm dance is underway; a song about 'The Fat Dog' is performed
jokes.punchline: The song insists 'it's not made up, it's not made up' — which is exactly what you'd say if it were made up — and the dance has an instructional component for a phrase nobody knows
jokes.explanation: The commitment to 'Fat Dog' as a full choreographed dance with a song is the ultimate payoff to the running gag. 'You've heard this expression your entire life / it's not made up, it's not made up' is structurally perfect — the song's insistence on its own legitimacy is the admission of its illegitimacy. The escalation from one-off joke to episode-ending musical number is very Community. High originality in the commitment to the bit.

jokes.text: It's a bear dance! Damn it.
jokes.setup: The Fat Dog dance is underway, apparently with costumes or moves that look like bears
jokes.punchline: Chang realizes (or someone accuses) that the Fat Dog dance looks exactly like a bear dance — connecting it back to the Wisconsin mauling — and his resigned 'Damn it' is the button
jokes.explanation: The final callback in the Bear/Fat Dog arc: the Fat Dog dance is indistinguishable from a bear dance, making Chang's entire workaround pointless. 'Damn it.' is the perfect one-word button. The structure — setup (Bear theme) → complication (mauling) → pivot (Fat Dog) → reveal (still a bear dance) — is four-act comedy construction compressed into an episode arc. Among the strongest structural payoffs in the episode.

jokes.text: For pencils, pens, and markers, press one. For tape, glue, and adhesives, press two. For staples, paper clips, and fasteners, press three. For marigold, press four.
jokes.setup: The episode's tag: someone is calling Greendale Faculty Office Supply — presumably to order a simple office item
jokes.punchline: The standard menu items (pencils, tape, staples) are followed by 'For marigold, press four' — a color that is not an office supply, presented with identical cadence and gravity
jokes.explanation: The post-credits tag is a masterclass in absurdist escalation via phone menu. The rhythm of three normal items followed by 'marigold' (a color, not a supply) is perfectly constructed. Then it continues: marigold → obsidian → aqua cerulean → arcadia → 'Enter activation code' → 'Confirmed. Arcadia initiated.' → 'What's your clearance level?' → 'Top.' This escalates from a mundane phone tree into what appears to be a shadow government conspiracy hidden inside Greendale's office supply line. The comedy is entirely structural.

jokes.text: Marigold. For obsidian, press one. For aqua cerulean, press two. For arcadia, press three.
jokes.setup: The caller has pressed 4 for marigold — now inside a submenu of colors
jokes.punchline: The submenu is entirely colors (obsidian, aqua cerulean, arcadia) — still presented as office supply options — the escalation from one rogue color to an entire submenu of colors reveals the depth of the conspiracy
jokes.explanation: Part of the same tag sequence as #80 — separated for scoring because each revelation is a distinct comedic beat. The color submenu's specificity (not just 'blue' but 'aqua cerulean') is excellent.

jokes.text: Enter activation code. — [tone] — Confirmed. Arcadia initiated. — What's your clearance level? — Top.
jokes.setup: The color submenu leads to an activation code prompt
jokes.punchline: 'Confirmed. Arcadia initiated.' — the office supply phone line has revealed itself as the front for a shadow operation. 'Clearance level: Top.'
jokes.explanation: The full payoff of the tag sequence. What started as a mundane phone menu has become a spy thriller activation sequence — 'Arcadia initiated,' 'What's your clearance level? Top.' This is Community's tag at its most brilliantly absurdist. The commitment to the bit through several layers of phone menu before the reveal is structurally impeccable. The joke is entirely about the reveal's incongruity with the setup (office supplies) and the deadpan authority of 'Arcadia initiated.' Near the top of the episode's scoring.

jokes.text: Oh, no, no. Cancel it. Wait. Who are you? Who is this? It's not... I'm... Right in front of you, stupid.
jokes.setup: The caller ('Top' clearance) panics and tries to cancel 'Arcadia'
jokes.punchline: An unknown voice reveals themselves to be 'right in front of you, stupid' — implying a face-to-face conspiracy encounter has been conducted through a phone menu that both parties were calling simultaneously, or that the shadow operative was physically present the whole time
jokes.explanation: 'Right in front of you, stupid.' is an inspired button — it suggests the entire phone-tree conspiracy ritual was conducted between two people standing in the same room, making the elaborate spy protocol maximum absurdist comedy. The episode ends on this note of complete institutional absurdity, rhyming with the bureaucratic labyrinth of the main plot.

tmdb_overview: While Annie and Hickey's fight to get a bulletin board repaired spirals out of control, Abed and Britta go to war over spoilers of his favorite show.
insight: Cork-based networking stumbles at 73.9: character comedy can't sustain absurdist premise alone.
